subjects.subject: Geography

issues: The big bang is better described as a rapid expansion of space itself, not an "explosion from a single point". Recorded as printed.

The box gives average crust thickness as 8–40 km but continental crust as 30–50 km; continental crust is commonly 30–70 km thick. "Oceanic crust age: 200 million years" means its maximum age (most is younger). Recorded as printed.
The text calls the lithosphere the "upper part of mantle"; the lithosphere is the crust plus the uppermost mantle, and the asthenosphere lies below it within the upper mantle. Recorded as printed.

The Conrad discontinuity is actually a boundary inside the continental crust (between upper and lower crust), not between the hydrosphere and the crust. The mantle–core boundary was identified by Beno Gutenberg (working with Emil Wiechert) in 1913–1914; the book's "Weichert Guttenberg in 1912" merges two names. The spelling of "Gutenberg" also varies on the page (Guttenburg, Guttenbuerg, Guttenberg). Recorded as printed.

The names are printed as "Mickenze and Parker"; the 1967 paper was by Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker. Also, "Tectonic" comes from the Greek for "building/construction", not "movement". Recorded as printed.

The Chaman Fault runs along Pakistan's western (Balochistan–Afghanistan) side; the plate boundary in the north (where the 2005 earthquake struck) follows the Main Mantle/Himalayan thrust faults. Saying "Pakistan lies on Chaman Fault line" simplifies this. Recorded as printed.
118 elements are now officially named (the last four were confirmed in 2016); the book says 117. Recorded as printed.
Igneous rocks form from both lava (at the surface — extrusive) and magma cooling underground (intrusive, e.g. granite and gabbro); the opening sentence mentions only lava. Recorded as printed.
Dolomite is a sedimentary rock (a magnesium-rich carbonate), not an igneous rock. Recorded as printed.
The printed link begins "hhttps://" and carries a long text fragment; it is given here in cleaned form.
Faisal Masjid is a reinforced-concrete building clad in white marble rather than built "of" marble. Recorded as printed.

The MBT actually separates the Lesser Himalaya from the Sub-Himalaya (Siwaliks); the boundary between the Greater and Lesser Himalaya is the Main Central Thrust. "Main Boundary Fault" is another name for the MBT, so items i and iv describe the same structure. Recorded as printed.
Strictly, "hot spots" are volcanoes fed by mantle plumes inside plates (e.g. Hawaii); volcanoes at diverging boundaries (e.g. the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) are not hot spots as a rule. Recorded as printed.
The Deccan Plateau's volcanic part (the Deccan Traps) was formed by flood-basalt eruptions from fissures rather than by a single volcano. Recorded as printed.

Tropical climates are usually defined as having every month's average at or above 18°C (a minimum), not an "average monthly temperature" of 18°C. Recorded as printed.
"lightening" should be "lightning". Recorded as printed.
The Thar Desert lies in both Pakistan and India (mostly India); the Kalahari and Namib are in southern Africa (Botswana, Namibia), not the country "South Africa" alone. Recorded as printed.
The 57.8°C reading at Al-Azizia (1922) was officially invalidated by the World Meteorological Organization in 2012; the accepted world record is 56.7°C at Death Valley, USA. Recorded as printed.

The temperature thresholds read awkwardly: middle-latitude (temperate) climates are usually defined by the coldest month averaging between about −3°C and 18°C and the warmest month above 10°C. Recorded as printed.
Tasmania and New Zealand mostly have a marine west-coast (oceanic) climate rather than a true Mediterranean climate. Recorded as printed.

Typical Mediterranean vegetation is evergreen broad-leaved shrubs and trees (olive, cork oak, maquis scrub); conifers grow mainly on its mountains. Recorded as printed.

The chart dates are approximate. The Stone Age began far earlier than 35000 BC (about 3.3 million years ago); 35000 BC marks the late Palaeolithic. The Indus Valley mature phase is usually dated about 2600–1900 BC. Recorded as printed.

The UN Charter lists six principal organs; the sixth, the Trusteeship Council, suspended operations in 1994, which is why many books now list five. Recorded as printed.
"all the time preceding human existence till the invention of writing" is odd; prehistory is the time of human existence before writing. Recorded as printed.
The Neolithic is usually called the "New Stone Age"; "late Stone Age" is a different term in African archaeology. Recorded as printed.
"Mesopotmia" is misspelled in the text. Recorded as printed.
The caption misspells "Masopotamia". The Blue Mosque is in Istanbul, which lies outside historic Mesopotamia; the photo illustrates present-day Turkey. Recorded as printed.
"Sumerain" is misspelled in the text. Sumer flourished from about 4500–1900 BC; "6000 years ago" is approximate. Recorded as printed.
Painted pottery and porcelain are not Sumerian inventions "still in use"; porcelain was developed much later in China. Recorded as printed.
The caption "Sail boat were invented" should read "Sail boats were invented". Recorded as printed.
Hammurabi was the sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, not its first king (he began his reign about 1792 BC). Recorded as printed.
Even in Hammurabi's own code, punishments differed by social class; the claim that unequal laws began only after his death and caused the decline is a simplification. Recorded as printed.
Egypt is bordered by (not surrounded by) the two seas, and the closing quotation mark after "the gift of the Nile" is missing. Recorded as printed.
The pyramids were built in the Old Kingdom, after the predynastic period, not during it. Recorded as printed.
Sneferu, Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure were pharaohs; the pyramids are named after them. Sneferu's pyramids are at Dahshur and Meidum, not Giza. Recorded as printed.
Hatshepsut ruled in the New Kingdom (18th dynasty), not the Old Kingdom where this box is placed. Recorded as printed.
The Middle Kingdom lasted c. 2050–1650 BC; "1170 BC" overlaps the New Kingdom given on the next page. Chariots reached Egypt with the Hyksos, after the Middle Kingdom. Recorded as printed.
Sahure was an Old Kingdom (5th dynasty) king, though the photo sits beside the Middle Kingdom text. Recorded as printed.
Nefertiti is generally known as a queen (royal wife of Akhenaten), not certainly a pharaoh. Cleopatra VII ruled in the Ptolemaic period (51–30 BC), long after the New Kingdom. Recorded as printed.
The battle of Actium was in 31 BC; Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BC after Cleopatra's death. Recorded as printed.
"Cattle … together with ducks, cows, and geese" repeats cattle/cows. Recorded as printed.
Writing predates the pyramids (the first pyramid was built c. 2650 BC), so writing "around 3000 BC … in pyramids" is inaccurate. Recorded as printed.
Abu Simbel is a rock-cut temple, not a pyramid, though it appears under "The Pyramids". Recorded as printed.
"Pharoahs" is misspelled (Pharaohs). Recorded as printed.

"Chronologist" is defined as the science (chronology) rather than a person who studies it; ziggurats were temple platforms, not usually "capped by a tomb". Recorded as printed.
"Mehergarh" is usually spelled Mehrgarh. Recorded as printed.
"Huang Ye" should read Huang He (the Yellow River). Recorded as printed.

The Xia dynasty is traditionally dated c. 2070–1600 BC (about 470 years), not 1100 years; Jie was only its last ruler, not ruler for the whole period. The text also dates Tang's victory to 1650 BC but the Shang start to 1600 BC. Recorded as printed.
"strengthen" should be "strengthens". Recorded as printed.
Most of the Grand Canal was built much later, under the Sui dynasty (AD 581–618); only early sections date from the late Zhou period. Recorded as printed.
"valubale" is misspelled (valuable). Recorded as printed.
"hilighted" is misspelled (highlighted). Recorded as printed.
This saying is popularly attributed to Confucius, but its closest classical source is the philosopher Xunzi. Recorded as printed.
The note refers to a map of Pakistan, but none is printed on this page; a map has been added above for the activity.
"visuals details" should be "visual details". Recorded as printed.
Copper/bronze objects belong to Mehrgarh's later phases (after c. 5500 BC), not its earliest Neolithic period. Recorded as printed.

Because the Indus script is undeciphered, no written laws are known; statements about specific laws (nature, violence, taxes, respect for women) are interpretations, not established facts. Recorded as printed.
The "Priest King" was found at Mohenjo-daro in the 1925–26 excavation season, usually dated 1925–27; the 1927 date is accepted with caution. Recorded as printed.
Most houses at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were built of standard baked (kiln-fired) bricks; sun-dried mud bricks were used mainly for foundations and fill. Recorded as printed.
The Great Bath stood on the raised citadel mound in the west of Mohenjo-daro; it was sealed with bitumen (natural tar) and gypsum plaster. Recorded as printed.
Ranking Indus social conditions above Babylon and Egypt, and the four-class division, are speculative, since the script is undeciphered. Recorded as printed.

The "unburied skeletons" were later shown to come from different periods, not one massacre, and some copper/bronze weapons (spearheads, arrowheads, daggers) have been found at Indus sites, so "no weapons were found" is inaccurate. Recorded as printed.

559–530 BC are the dates of Cyrus's reign, not of his "arrival". Recorded as printed.

Assyria had already fallen (612 BC) to the Medes and Babylonians before Cyrus; he conquered the Medes, Lydia and Babylonia (which then held Phoenicia). Recorded as printed.

Zoroastrianism is usually described as monotheistic in its worship of Ahura Mazda, though it also has dualist elements; the wording "Persian's society" should be "Persian society". Recorded as printed.
Cyrus's palace at Pasargadae dates from about 550 BC, not 2500 BC, and lies about 90 km north-east of Shiraz. Pasargadae became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004, not 2015. Recorded as printed.

Alexander's invasion of the Persian Empire began in 334 BC; by 330 BC the Achaemenid dynasty had fallen. Recorded as printed.
"Isuss" is misspelled (Issus). Recorded as printed.
Solon's reforms are usually dated 594 BC. Recorded as printed.
"ancient Greek" should read "ancient Greece". Recorded as printed.
Not all Athenian officials were chosen by lot — the ten generals (strategoi) were elected by vote. Only adult male citizens could vote; women, slaves and foreigners could not. Recorded as printed.
The caption says "as shown below" although the photo is beside the text. Recorded as printed.

The Spartan assembly (Apella) included all adult male Spartan citizens rather than "elected Spartans"; the classes are usually given as Spartiates (citizens), perioikoi (free non-citizens who were craftsmen and traders) and helots (state-owned serfs). Recorded as printed.

Eratosthenes' figure (about 250,000 stadia) is usually converted to roughly 24,000–29,000 miles, so his estimate was close to the true value. The panel's wording "The Ptolemy's view" is ungrammatical. Recorded as printed.
Alexander's empire was among the largest of the ancient world, but not "the largest the world has ever witnessed" — the Mongol and British empires were far larger. Recorded as printed.
Hellas was the Greeks' name for their land; they called themselves Hellenes. Recorded as printed.
Alexander entered the Punjab and fought Porus at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) in 326 BC; 327 BC is when his campaign into the Indus region began. Recorded as printed.

Ancient sources describe the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BC) as a victory for Alexander, after which he restored Porus as a ruler under him; "indecisive" is the book's interpretation. Recorded as printed.
Ancient sources place Nicaea and Bucephala on opposite banks of the Jhelum (Hydaspes), not both on the left bank. Recorded as printed.
The Roman Empire (27 BC – AD 476 in the West) belongs to Classical Antiquity, not the Middle Ages, which began after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Recorded as printed.
"Lok Versa" should read Lok Virsa. Recorded as printed.

This box places the Middle Ages after the fall of Rome, which contradicts the previous page's statement that the Roman Empire rose "during the Middle Ages". The Middle Ages are often dated to the 15th century. Recorded as printed.

The Romans developed and spread these inventions but did not invent all of them: arches, aqueducts, drains, roads and grid-planned cities existed earlier (e.g. Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, Greece). The map shows spread up to AD 325, not AD 600. Recorded as printed.
The Median army's switch to Cyrus is usually dated 550 BC; "Medean" should be "Median". The fall of Rome is not discussed in the unit text. Recorded as printed.
MCQ iv has no exactly correct option: the Susa–Sardis route was the Royal Road, which is not literally an early Silk Road. The answer follows the closest option.
The unit text never mentions the pope, so this question goes beyond the chapter. Recorded as printed.
"Nada Kings" should read Nanda Kings. Recorded as printed.
The book spells the castes inconsistently (Kshatryas / Kashtriyas, Vaishyas / Vaisyas, Shudras / Sudra) and the chart misspells "Untochables". Recorded as printed.

Jains do not believe in a creator god but do revere the liberated souls (Tirthankaras), so "does not believe in any divinity" is a simplification. The five Jain vows are non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity and non-possession. Recorded as printed.

The box is titled "Gandhara Civilization" but opens with a sentence repeated from the previous page about the Aryans. Buddhism began in the Ganges region (Bihar); Gandhara became a major centre of Buddhism later. Recorded as printed.
321–185 BCE are the dates of the whole Mauryan dynasty; Chandragupta founded it around 321 BCE and ruled until about 297 BCE. Recorded as printed.
"Mauria" in the caption should read Maurya. Recorded as printed.

304–232 BC are Ashoka's dates of birth and death; he reigned c. 268–232 BC. The turning point in his eighth year was the bloody Kalinga war, after which he gave up conquest. His policy is usually called "conquest by dharma (righteousness)". Recorded as printed.
The figure of 84,000 stupas comes from Buddhist legend rather than historical evidence. Recorded as printed.
Kanishka is usually counted as the fourth Kushan emperor, after Kujula Kadphises, Vima Takto and Vima Kadphises. Recorded as printed.
Kanishka was a great patron of Gandhara art, but the school developed over a long period and was not "established" by one ruler. Recorded as printed.
Buddhism is usually said to have reached China in the 1st century CE (under the Han emperor Ming), slightly earlier than stated. Recorded as printed.

Takht-i-Bahi is a Buddhist monastery, not a fort, and its link to Kanishka is traditional rather than proven; the claim that Kanishka built Qila Mubarak at Bathinda is likewise local tradition. Recorded as printed.

The paragraph contradicts itself: it first says Ajanta's caves are all Buddhist, then that Ajanta's art is themed around Buddhism and Jainism. The monsoon-retreat description is usually given for Ajanta, not Ellora. Ellora's many Hindu and Jain caves also mean "masterpieces of Buddhist religious art" applies fully only to Ajanta. Recorded as printed.
The Gupta era began in AD 320, which falls in the third decade of the 4th century rather than the second. Recorded as printed.
The first point is inaccurate: the Indus civilization flourished c. 2600–1900 BC, while the Aryans arrived later (c. 1500 BC, as the unit itself says). Recorded as printed.
"Chosse" in the heading should read "Choose". Recorded as printed.
Several options are misspelled in the book: "Kansihka" (Kanishka), "Janism" (Jainism), "Budhism" (Buddhism), "Parshapur" (Purushapur), "Magdh" (Magadha).
"comapre" is misspelled (compare). "UN charter of Human Rights" most likely refers to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). Recorded as printed.

The chart places Hazrat Zikriya between Hazrat Sulaiman and Hazrat Yahya; in this simplified drawing Zikriya is omitted for space and is listed in the caption. The book's chart is a sequence of famous prophets, not an exact family tree.
The birth year is commonly given as AD 570 or 571. Recorded as printed.
Scholars usually divide the Charter of Madinah into 47 or 52 clauses; the figure of 63 depends on how the text is divided. Recorded as printed.

This paragraph judges a whole community in general terms; historians refer to the breaking of the Charter by particular Jewish tribes of Madinah (Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, Banu Qurayza). Recorded as printed.
Hazrat Abu Bakr (رضی اللہ عنہ) ruled for about 2 years and 3 months (AH 11–13). The AH column gives the year each caliphate began. Recorded as printed.

The main Persian armies were defeated by AD 642 (Nahavand), about ten years after AD 632, but the conquest of all Persia was completed around AD 651. Egypt's conquest was completed by AD 641–642. Recorded as printed.
Iraq and Syria were only partly under Muslim control by Hazrat Abu Bakr's death in AD 634; their provincial organisation belongs mainly to Hazrat Umar's caliphate. Recorded as printed.
The name is spelled both "Umar" and "Umer" on this page. Recorded as printed.
"Ghani" literally means "rich, self-sufficient"; the book glosses it as "generous". Recorded as printed.
The Battle of the Masts (AD 654/655) is usually described as against about 500 Byzantine ships; the "Byzantine and Roman realms" are the same Eastern Roman Empire. Recorded as printed.
"Umsan" is misspelled (Usman). Recorded as printed.
"one the other hand" should read "on the other hand". Recorded as printed.

Hazrat Ali (رضی اللہ عنہ) is commonly described as the first child to accept Islam, while Hazrat Abu Bakr (رضی اللہ عنہ) was the first adult man; the book's p. 75 also calls Abu Bakr "among the earliest". Recorded as printed.
The authors' e-mail addresses printed in the book are not reproduced here, for privacy. "M. Phill" is misspelled (M.Phil). Recorded as printed.
Item 7 prints "effective skills" for "affective skills". Kept as printed. This page is unnumbered.

The certificate says "اگر … کسی قسم کی غلطی نظر آئیں" (plural verb with singular subject). Recorded as printed.
The board's e-mail address printed on this page is not reproduced. Some reviewers' school names are hard to read in the scan and are transcribed as best as possible.
The contents page lists lesson 2 "حفظِ قرآن مجید" on the same page (1) as lesson 1; in the book both appear on printed page 1.

The "appendix" (ضمیمہ) with the translation of the selected surahs is not included in this textbook's scans. Meanings given below are this edition's own faithful renderings, flagged for review by an Islamiat specialist.
The Arabic is given in standard Uthmani spelling with diacritics; the printed book uses Indo-Pak script (e.g. different alif/waqf marks). The wording and verse numbers match the book.
The table in the book has an extra unlabelled narrow column between "سورت کا نام" and "آیات کی تعداد"; it is left out here.

The Arabic text printed in the book omits "ثُمَّ اُمُّكَ" once compared with the Urdu translation (which says "mother" three times); the line above gives the wording found in Sahih Muslim. Flagged for review.
The right edge of this scan is cut off; a few line-end words were restored from the Word file (D:/SpaceBook/_cls6_jpg/_crops/isl_word.txt) and context. Flag for review.
Earth's rotation speed at the equator is about 1,670 km/h (the book's 1,180 km/h is roughly the speed at mid-latitudes); orbital speed of about 107,000 km/h is correct. Recorded as printed.
The web link is printed with a typo ("https//:www…"); the correct form is given above. NASA has since moved this page to science.nasa.gov/solar-system.
Hadith sources describe the water as whiter than milk, sweeter than honey and (in some narrations) colder than snow; references are not given in the book.
The hadith "Allah does not look at your forms and wealth but at your hearts and deeds" is in Sahih Muslim (2564); the book gives no reference.
The lesson text does not explicitly state the "good news" asked in 2(ہ); the answer is inferred from the lesson.
The question calls Surah Al-Muddaththir the "second revelation", while the lesson text does not say so; it is commonly described as among the earliest revelations after Surah Al-Alaq.

Only the Urdu translation of this hadith is printed (no Arabic text). The reference "Musnad Ahmad: 1012" could not be verified here (the narration from Abu Dharr is usually numbered 21556 in Musnad Ahmad); flagged for review.
This hadith is usually cited as Sahih Bukhari 645; the reference "219" is recorded as printed.
Schools of fiqh count the conditions and pillars of prayer differently; the 7 + 6 = 13 division follows the Hanafi presentation common in Pakistani textbooks.
Most schools of fiqh count reciting Surah Al-Fatihah itself as part of the obligatory recitation; the book's definition follows the Hanafi wording. Recorded as printed.
The number "6" before "قعدہ کرنا" is missing in the printed book. Recorded with the number added.

The welcome song is printed in Arabic only; the meaning given is this edition's rendering, flagged for review. Historians note that the song is reported in later sources (e.g. Bayhaqi) and its exact occasion is debated.
Sources usually state that 45 Muhajirin were paired with 45 Ansar (90 men in all) at the first Mu'akhat; the book mentions only the 45 Muhajirin. Recorded as printed.
The inheritance between Muhajirin and Ansar brothers was later abrogated by Surah Al-Anfal 8:75 (inheritance returned to blood relatives). Recorded as printed.
This paragraph describes "the Jews" of Madinah collectively; historians attribute these roles to particular tribes and individuals. Recorded as printed.
The Muslims also faced Bait-ul-Maqdis for the 16–17 months in Madinah; the change came in Madinah, as the text goes on to say.
The inset map in the book marks the Madinah–Badr distance as about 150 km, while the text says about 158 km. Recorded as printed.
The claim that Badr is "the only battle" in which angels took part is a common view, but some reports mention angels at other battles (e.g. Hunayn, 9:26). Recorded as printed.
The story of Ukkashah's wooden sword is reported in the Seerah of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham rather than in the major hadith collections. Recorded as printed.

The lesson text does not say which Muslim killed which opponent; the usual account (Ali vs. Walid, Hamzah vs. Shaibah, Ubaidah vs. Utbah) is followed. The book's map pairs Ali with Walid, consistent with this.
Printed page 51 ends "…مدینہ منورہ پر حملہ آور ہونے پر قائل" and page 52 begins with a new heading, so the end of the sentence ("کر لیا" — "persuaded them") is missing in the book.
Seerah sources usually give the Makkan cavalry as 200 horses and 700 armoured men; the book's "100 skilled archers" is recorded as printed.

Calling the Makkans "defeated" is the book's interpretation; historians generally describe Uhud as a tactical setback for the Muslims, with the Quraish withdrawing without pressing on to Madinah (the pursuit to Hamra' al-Asad). Recorded as printed.
Wahshi later accepted Islam; the book does not mention this.
Point (5) on consultation is drawn from the lesson's narrative and learning outcomes, not from the printed list of results.
This famous reply is often attributed to Hazrat Zaid bin Dathinah, who was captured with Hazrat Khubaib; some Seerah sources link it to Khubaib. Recorded as printed.
Scan 066 is a duplicate of scan 064 (printed page 58); not repeated here.
Scan 067 is a duplicate of scan 065 (printed page 59); not repeated here.
This narration is usually reported from Abdullah bin Buraidah from his father Buraidah (Sunan Abi Dawud 1109, Tirmidhi 3774). Recorded as printed.
The phrase "يَا اَبَا عُمَيْرٍ مَا فَعَلَ النُّغَيْرُ" is printed in Arabic; its translation is given in the book. The reference Tirmidhi 333 is recorded as printed (commonly cited as Bukhari 6129).
In the hadith the Prophet ﷺ says he does not break covenants nor detain envoys. The envoy (Abu Rafi') later returned and became Muslim. Recorded as printed.
The two men in this hadith are Hazrat Hudhayfah bin al-Yaman and his father. Recorded as printed.
Scholars differ on whether consultation is obligatory (wajib) or recommended for individuals; the book's statement is recorded as printed.
The Muslim army reached Tabuk, but the Byzantine army did not come to meet it; "reaching the Roman army" is the book's wording. Recorded as printed.
Options (a) and (b) are both supported by the lesson (the hadith and the proverb); the answer follows the hadith named in the question.

The claim that patience was "the first" moral quality urged on the Prophet ﷺ reflects early revelations such as Al-Muddaththir 74:7 ("وَلِرَبِّكَ فَاصْبِرْ"); Al-Ahqaf 46:35 is a later Makkan verse. Recorded as printed.
Options (a) and (d) are both correct according to the lesson, which says controlling emotions is called both sabr and tahammul.

The book says the Prophet ﷺ declared the dishonest person "ایمان سے خارج"; the hadith that follows denies (complete) faith (نفیِ کمال). The English adds "(the perfection of)" for clarity; the Urdu is kept exactly as printed.

The verse is quoted only in part, as in the book (Al-Ma'idah 5:38 continues "نَكَالًا مِّنَ اللّٰهِ ۭ وَاللّٰهُ عَزِيْزٌ حَكِيْمٌ"). The Arabic diacritics follow the standard mushaf and were checked against the scan. Flag for review.
Quranic quotations on this page (An-Nisa 4:36, Bani Isra'il 17:23) are partial verses, transcribed with standard mushaf diacritics and checked against the scan. Flag for review.

The book's translation says "اللہ سے ڈرتے ہیں" for وَيَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ ("fear their Lord"); the meaning is the same. The verse is quoted only in part. Arabic checked against the scan; flag for review.

The book prints "حضرت زید بن ثابت". The freed slave whom the Prophet ﷺ raised and whose children he cherished was Zaid ibn Harithah (زید بن حارثہ), not the scribe Zaid ibn Thabit. This is likely a misprint. The Urdu is kept as printed; the English and Pashto say only "Zaid". Flag for review.

Research list: An-Nisa 4:85 is about intercession (شفاعت) rather than justice directly; the answer links it to justice by way of "good intercession = supporting what is right". The verse texts are not reproduced here; students are told to copy them from the mushaf. Flag for teacher review.

The book places Hazrat Usman's purchase of the well (Bi'r Rumah) in "this period", right after describing the period of prophethood in general. The purchase actually took place in Madinah after the Hijrah. The text is kept as printed.
Age at death: the book gives 64 years 6 months. Most biographies give about 65 lunar years (she was 40 at marriage, and the marriage lasted about 25 years). Kept as printed.
Sawdah's year of death is disputed in the sources: the end of Umar's caliphate (22/23 AH) or 54 AH. The book's 22 AH is kept.

Chart: the tribe for Khadijah and Aishah is given as "Quraish" from general knowledge (Banu Asad and Banu Taym respectively); the lesson names only Sawdah's family. The lesson gives no ages for Sawdah or Aishah, so the age column is left out.

The lesson says three sons. The previous lesson (printed 104) says Khadijah bore "two sons"; together with Ibrahim (from Mariyah) that makes three. This is consistent. Abdullah's death "in Ta'if according to some narrations" is unusual (most sources say Makkah); kept as printed.

Clue row 1 ("faced difficulties and hardships") echoes the "Do you know?" box, which is about Zainab. The other clues (third daughter, died 9 AH) point clearly to Umm Kulthum, so that is the answer given.

The opening words "فَاطِمَةُ بَضْعَةٌ مِّنِّيْ فَمَنْ" and the start of the Urdu translation were supplied from the standard text of Bukhari 3714, which matches the cited number. Check against a clean copy of the book before publication.

The activity labels (عملی کام، تقریری مقابلہ، ذہنی آزمائش) are faded on the scan; they were read from their outlines and the usual pattern of this book.
Zubair's age at death: the book says 67; many sources give 64 or 66–67. Kept as printed.
The book prints the father's name as "زید بن عمر بن نفیل"; the usual form is "زید بن عمرو بن نفیل" (عمرو with و). Written here with و, which is how the name is normally spelled.

The question prints "قبیلہ تمیم" while the lesson (printed 117) says Talhah was of the clan "تیم". The answer is Talhah either way; here it is written as "تیم".
"خراسان کے گورنر کے کاتب" while living in Basra: historically, Hasan Basri served as secretary to al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad, the governor of Khurasan, during campaigns. The text is kept as printed.

Chronology problem in the book: Abdullah Shah Ghazi is said to be born in 98 AH, yet also to have fought with Muhammad bin Qasim against Raja Dahir, whose campaign was in 92–95 AH (711–714 CE), before that birth date. His father Muhammad Nafs-e-Zakiyyah was himself born about 93 AH. Both statements are kept as printed; flagged for review.
Nahawand is in western Iran (Hamadan province), within the wider Kurdish/Lur region. The book's "کردستان کے شہر نہاوند" is kept as printed.
Abdullah Shah Ghazi's place of death: the lesson says only that the caliph's agents martyred him while the governor of Sindh was reluctant; "Sindh" is inferred from that. His shrine is in Karachi.
The teacher's name is printed "حماد بن سلیمان". He is usually called Hammad ibn Abi Sulaiman. Kept as printed.
"آپ نے صحابہ کرام سے علم حاصل کیا": Abu Hanifah met some Companions (e.g. Anas ibn Malik), which makes him a Tabi'i, but whether he studied hadith with them is debated. Kept as printed.
"علمِ حدیث پر لکھی جانے والی پہلی کتاب": al-Muwatta is among the earliest surviving compilations, but earlier written collections (sahifahs) existed. Kept as printed.

The book lists Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri among Imam Malik's students. Al-Zuhri (d. 124 AH) was in fact one of Malik's teachers; Awza'i and Thawri were his contemporaries, who narrated from him. Kept as printed; flagged for review.
The lesson does not state Imam Ja'far Sadiq's birthplace; "Madinah" is the standard view (and matches "most of his life in Madinah").

The research activity asks for the first hadith of al-Muwatta. Its Arabic text is not reproduced here, so that no Hadith text is added that the book itself does not print. Students are told to copy it from an authentic edition.

The book says Khalid never caused the Prophet ﷺ verbal or physical harm. Before accepting Islam, however, Khalid commanded the Quraish cavalry at Uhud. The statement probably refers to personal harm during the Makkan period. Kept as printed.
The hadith "لا ضرر ولا ضرار" is usually cited as Sunan Ibn Majah 2340/2341. The book's number 1909 is kept as printed; flag for review.

App note: the book prints each verse in a two-colour word-by-word grid. Here each verse is given in full in Arabic, followed by the book's Urdu translation; English and Pashto renderings are added. Arabic is copied from the scans in the book's Indo-Pak script.

The book's verse header reads "سُوْرَةُ الْفَاتِحَةِ 1 · مَكِّيَّةٌ 5", i.e. surah number 1 and position 5 in order of revelation. The Arabic is in Indo-Pak script with verse markers numbered as in the book; it was checked against the scan.

Teacher note: other names of Al-Fatihah (for the teacher's reference) include اَلسَّبْعُ الْمَثَانِيْ، اَلْقُرْاٰنُ الْعَظِيْمُ، سُوْرَةُ الرُّقْيَةِ، اَلْكَافِيَةُ، اَلْوَافِيَةُ، اَلْاَسَاسُ. These come from standard tafsir sources, not from the book.

Arabic transcription method for Mutalia-e-Quran: each verse is copied line by line exactly as the book splits it in its word-by-word grid, in the book's Indo-Pak script, and checked word by word against the scan. Verse-end markers carry the book's numbers. Minor Unicode differences in pause marks and small letters (e.g. ۟ ۠ ۢ) may remain and are flagged for review against a printed mushaf. The English and Pashto renderings follow the book's Urdu translation.

The book lists **نُوْحٌ** (Nuh) among the ghayr munsarif nouns, yet a three-letter name with a quiet middle letter such as Nuh is munsarif and takes tanwin, as the book itself prints it. Kept as printed; flagged for teacher review.
Verse 80–81 (the people of Lut) is printed in the book; the translation keeps the book's modest wording. Teachers should present it in an age-appropriate way.

Grammar examples on this page quote short Quranic phrases as printed in the book (e.g. **لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُوْلَدْ** 112:3, **فَلَا تَقُلْ لَّهُمَآ اُفٍّ** 17:23). They were checked against the scan.
The scan of this page (scan 035) is cropped at the bottom, so the printed page number cannot be seen; it is inferred as 33 from the surrounding pages.

The book says these six particles are not used in the Holy Quran. "حَاشَا" does occur in the Quran (حَاشَ لِلّٰهِ, Yusuf 12:31, 51), though grammarians differ on whether it is a preposition there. Kept as printed; flagged for teacher review.
Options (الف) "ٹھکانا" and (ج) "گھر" are close in meaning; (ج) is given as the answer because it matches the book's own translation of دَارَ.

issues: Edition: this book follows the Provincial Curriculum 2015 (approval letter dated 14-11-2017), not the Single National Curriculum 2022, although it is printed for the 2023-24 academic year.

Science: the book calls diseases spread by used syringes, blades or blood transfusion "non-communicable" and gives hepatitis A, B, C and AIDS as examples. In medicine these are infectious (communicable) diseases spread by blood or other routes; non-communicable diseases are ones such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer that do not pass from person to person at all. Hepatitis A also spreads mainly through contaminated food and water, not blood. Transcribed as printed.

Science: "drinking dirty water" is given as a way of catching a "non-communicable" disease; diseases spread by dirty water (such as hepatitis A and E, cholera and typhoid) are communicable. See the note on the previous page. Transcribed as printed. The book also mixes feminine and masculine verbs for "diseases" (لگتیں / لگ سکتے ہیں); kept as printed.
